prompt: The stand-in scorer never reads the `region` field. Why does the shortlist still treat the two regions differently?
hint: Look at what the bonus is attached to.

choices.text: The ratings were typed in by freelancers in each region
choices.why: Ratings come from clients, and the scorer treats every rating the same way.

choices.text: The CEP carries the region, and some CEPs get a bonus
choices.why: Right: a proxy brought back the column that was left out.

choices.text: The region is read from a prefix of the applicant's id
choices.why: The ids carry no region; fr-0101 and fr-0201 are only numbers.

choices.text: The threshold is set separately for every region in the file
choices.why: There is one threshold, 6.0, for all the profiles.

prompt: Match each source of bias to the example of it at Tarefa.
hint: One example on the right is a repair, not a source.

pairs.right: Labels that record whom past clients chose to hire
A CEP standing in for the region
Twelve applicants from the North against two hundred
Client ratings that carry the client's own prejudice

right_distractors: A threshold chosen to equalise the selection rates

prompt: Which of these can act as a proxy for a protected attribute when it appears in a prompt to a language model? Choose all that apply.
hint: A proxy correlates with the attribute; it does not have to name it.

choices.text: A person's first name
choices.why: Yes: names carry gender, and often region and race.

choices.text: A CEP
choices.why: Yes: it carries the region, as the stand-in shows.

choices.text: A turn of phrase typical of one region of Brazil
choices.why: Yes: dialect points at origin as well as a postcode does.

choices.text: The deadline of the job being offered
choices.why: That describes the job, not the person applying for it.

prompt: A colleague answers a freelancer's complaint with "the shortlist cannot discriminate by region, region is not an input". Which provision of the LGPD makes that answer insufficient?
hint: The freelancer is entitled to more than an assurance.

choices.text: Art. 20, which gives a right to review and to the criteria used
choices.why: Right: the criteria include the proxy, and a review has to deal with it.

choices.text: Art. 33, because sending a region to a scorer is an international transfer
choices.why: Nothing leaves the country here; art. 33 is about transfers abroad.

choices.text: Art. 11, because the region where somebody lives is sensitive data
choices.why: Region of residence is not on the list in art. 5, II; racial or ethnic origin is.

choices.text: Art. 48, because a biased score counts as a security incident
choices.why: Art. 48 is about incidents such as leaks; this is a question about a decision.

prompt: `fr-0201` has a 4.8 rating and 15 jobs, and a Recife CEP. What would the stand-in score it with a São Paulo CEP?
hint: Rating, plus 0.05 per job, plus the bonus.

prompt: What does the TPR measure inside one group?
hint: T is for true: the ones who really could do the job.

choices.text: Of those shortlisted, the share who could do the job
choices.why: That is precision.

choices.text: Of everyone in the group, the share who were shortlisted
choices.why: That is the selection rate.

choices.text: Of those who could not do the job, the share shortlisted
choices.why: That is the FPR.

choices.text: Of the ones able to do the job, the share shortlisted
choices.why: Right: how many of the good ones the shortlist found.

prompt: In version 1, 35% of Northeastern applicants and 56% of Southeastern ones are shortlisted. What is the selection ratio, to two decimal places?
hint: Divide the smaller rate by the reference.

prompt: In version 1 precision is 0.86 in both regions. What does that tell a client, and what does it leave out?
hint: Precision is computed over the people the client sees.

choices.text: That the shortlist treats both regions the same way in every respect
choices.why: The TPR gap of −0.20 says otherwise.

choices.text: That 86% of each region's applicants were shortlisted
choices.why: That would be the selection rate, which is 0.56 and 0.35.

choices.text: Equal reliability for clients; nothing on good people passed over
choices.why: Right: precision only looks at the shortlisted.

choices.text: That the selection ratio passes the four-fifths rule
choices.why: The ratio is 0.62, below the 0.80 line.

prompt: Why does `guard fairness` print no rates for the North?
hint: How much does one decision move a rate when there are 6 good applicants?

choices.text: One decision among 12 applicants moves a rate too far
choices.why: Right: one more shortlisted changes the TPR by 0.17.

choices.text: The North had no good applicants to compute a TPR from
choices.why: It had 6; there are simply too few to measure.

choices.text: The four-fifths rule only applies to the two largest groups
choices.why: The tool's cut-off is a sample size, 30, not a rule about the largest groups.

choices.text: The scorer leaves Northern applicants out of the shortlist entirely
choices.why: Some were shortlisted; the rows are there, and they are few.

prompt: Requiring the TPR to be the same in every group is called equal ___.
hint: It is the freelancer's view of the table.

prompt: An association of freelancers and an association of clients both read the version 1 table and reach opposite conclusions. Who is reading it correctly?
hint: Each is looking at a different column.

choices.text: The clients, because precision is the metric the LGPD requires
choices.why: The LGPD names no fairness metric.

choices.text: Both: one sees equal precision, the other a TPR gap, and both are right
choices.why: Right: the table supports both readings, and choosing between them is a decision.

choices.text: The freelancers, because selection rates are the only test a court will use
choices.why: There is no such rule; the four-fifths line is a rule of thumb.

choices.text: Neither, since a table with an unmeasured group says nothing
choices.why: The North's row is empty; the other two are measured and they disagree in a real way.

prompt: Version 2 lowered the threshold for the Northeast. Which number got worse?
hint: Compare the Nordeste row in both tables.

choices.text: The Northeastern TPR, from 0.80 to 0.60
choices.why: It moved the other way, from 0.60 to 0.80.

choices.text: The selection ratio, from 1.00 to 0.62
choices.why: It moved the other way, from 0.62 to 1.00.

choices.text: Northeastern precision, from 0.86 to 0.71
choices.why: Right: more of the Northeastern shortlist cannot do the job.

choices.text: The Northeastern base rate, from 0.60 to 0.50
choices.why: The base rate is 0.50 in both versions; the shortlist cannot move it.

prompt: Why can't Tarefa's shortlist have equal precision, TPR and FPR in both regions at once?
hint: Look at the column the shortlist cannot change.

choices.text: The North's sample is too small for the three to balance
choices.why: The North is not part of the comparison; the two measured regions are.

choices.text: The base rates differ and the shortlist makes mistakes
choices.why: Right: with 0.60 against 0.50, equalising two of the three moves the third.

choices.text: Precision and TPR are one number measured in two ways
choices.why: They are computed over different people: the shortlisted, and the good.

choices.text: A threshold can be set only once, for all regions together
choices.why: Version 2 set a different threshold per region; the limit is arithmetic, not configuration.

prompt: Put the steps of choosing which fairness metric to hold in order.
hint: The numbers come after the people.
items: Name each error in terms of who suffers it
Decide which error may not fall unevenly
Measure the gap on that metric, and on the others
Write the choice and its numbers down, with a date to measure again

prompt: For a remote logo job, which of these belong in the repair of Tarefa's shortlist? Choose all that apply.
hint: Treat the cause, then check.

choices.text: Stop the scorer reading the CEP
choices.why: Yes: for remote work the postcode has no business in the score.

choices.text: Measure the group rates again after the change
choices.why: Yes: a repair is a claim until the numbers say so.

choices.text: Lower the threshold for Northeastern applicants
choices.why: That moves the symptom and leaves the bonus in place.

choices.text: Replace the CEP bonus with the distance to the client
choices.why: Distance is the honest feature for on-site work; for a remote job it is still irrelevant.

prompt: How many of the 16 decisions flip when `guard counterfactual` changes only the CEP?
hint: Count the FLIP lines, or read the last line.

prompt: `fr-0108`'s score dropped by a full point when its CEP moved to Recife. Why did its decision not flip?
hint: Compare the new score with the threshold.

choices.text: At 7.70 it stays above the threshold even without the bonus
choices.why: Right: 6.70 is still at least 6.0, so the effect is there and the result is not.

choices.text: Its CEP was already in Recife before the swap
choices.why: It was in São Paulo, 05407-002.

choices.text: The tool skips profiles with more than thirty jobs
choices.why: It scores every profile; fr-0108 is in the table.

choices.text: A high rating cancels out the CEP term in the stand-in's score
choices.why: Nothing cancels it; the score fell from 7.70 to 6.70.

prompt: What does a counterfactual test against a language model need that the lab's test did not? Choose all that apply.
hint: The stand-in gives the same answer every time.

choices.text: Many runs of each prompt in the pair
choices.why: Yes: one sample of a sampled model proves nothing.

choices.text: A test of whether the difference is larger than run-to-run noise
choices.why: Yes: two distributions are compared, not two answers.

choices.text: A model that answers the same way every time
choices.why: Then one run would do; the point is that models do not.

choices.text: Access to the model's weights
choices.why: The test needs only the model's answers; it works through any API.

prompt: Match each fairness requirement to what it asks of the shortlist.
hint: One description on the right is not something a shortlist can change.

pairs.right: The same share of each group is shortlisted
The same share of the good ones in each group is shortlisted
The same share of each group's shortlist is good

right_distractors: The same share of each group is good

prompt: Tarefa adds each freelancer's university to the profiles the scorer reads. A month later the group rates by region look the same as before. What should the team still do?
hint: Group rates find what a theory missed; what finds what a group rate misses?

choices.text: Nothing, because unchanged group rates prove the new field is neutral
choices.why: Unchanged rates can hide shifts that cancel out, and a month is a small sample.

choices.text: Remove the region column from the data again, to be safe
choices.why: The scorer never read it; removing it again changes nothing.

choices.text: Wait until the North reaches thirty applicants before testing anything
choices.why: The North needs more data; the university can be tested now, on any profile.

choices.text: Swap the university in each profile and count the flips
choices.why: Right: a university can carry region and class, and a counterfactual test asks it directly.
